title: Rose and Martin
hookLine: a broom and a garden hut: the saints of Lima were both Dominican

lines: A HUT IN A FAMILY GARDEN.
cards: Two objects from one city. The first is a broom. It belongs to a Dominican brother in Lima, in Peru, who sweeps the cloister, the infirmary and the kitchen every day.
The city nicknames him Brother Broom. The second is a tiny hut at the bottom of a family garden in the same city, barely big enough to kneel in.
A young woman prays there among the flowers she grows and sells to help her family. The broom belonged to Martin de Porres, the hut to Rose of Lima. Today, two saints, one city, one white habit.

teach.h: LIMA: A CITY SORTED BY RANK.
teach.b: You met each in year three; today, both together. Lima under Spanish rule was a city of Spaniards, Indigenous Peruvians, Africans enslaved and free, and people of mixed ancestry, sorted by strict lines of rank.
Martin was born on the wrong side of those lines. His father was a Spanish nobleman; his mother, a free woman of African descent.

teach.h: MARTIN: A HELPER, THEN A BROTHER.
teach.b: When he asked to join the Dominicans, he was taken in as a helper, not a full brother. He swept. He cut hair.
He nursed the sick in the priory and the streets, and gave away whatever came into his hands. Stories gathered around him, including his gentleness with animals, even the priory's mice.
In time the brothers received him as a lay brother. Rose took a different road to the same family.

teach.h: ROSE: A LAYWOMAN AT HOME, LIKE CATHERINE.
teach.b: Like Catherine of Siena, the mantellata, she stayed home as a Dominican laywoman, and tradition says she took Catherine as her model.
Her needle and garden supported her parents, and part of the house became a place to care for the sick and poor.
She also practiced hard penances that can be difficult to read about today, and her biographers don't hide them. Tradition says Rose and Martin knew each other.

teach.h: CHRIST IN THE PEOPLE LIMA LOOKED PAST.
teach.b: Each found Christ in the people their city looked past.

teach.h: ONE OF THESE MY LEAST BRETHREN.
teach.b: Jesus says it plainly in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

how: Catholics in Peru and far beyond honor Saint Rose of Lima and Saint Martin de Porres with feast days, processions and prayers; Dominican churches in Lima keep their shrines.

games.q: you're a young man of mixed ancestry in Lima. the priory will take you, but only as a helper, not as a brother. what do you do?
o: accept, and serve with the broom and the sick.
refuse to come unless you're made a full brother.
games.why: Martin took the helper's place. he swept, cut hair and nursed the sick, and in time the brothers received him as a lay brother.

practice: Bring Peru to mind, whatever you know of it, the coast and the mountains, the markets of Lima, a Peruvian neighbor, a dish you love, and hold its people for a few breaths.

Then picture a broom and a garden, ordinary work offered; if you pray, ask Saint Rose and Saint Martin to pray for Peru and for the people their city overlooked, and if not, hold Peru in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Rose and Martin. Rose of Lima, a Dominican laywoman in a garden hut, and Martin de Porres, the brother with the broom: two Dominican saints of one city. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: Brother Broom, the nickname people in Lima gave Martin de Porres.

carryVoice: Your line: lima's saints. A broom and a garden, and Christ in the people the city passed by. Go gently.
